title: Data compression: Huffman coding and run length encoding

tips.title: Frequency first, then the data
tips.body: An RLE pair is **how many**, then **what**: `3 1` means three 1s. A run of one still needs its own pair, so `1c` is not written as `c`. Check the frequencies add up to the length of the original.

tips.title: Frequency times code length, added up
tips.body: Every Huffman bit calculation is the same: multiply each character's frequency by the **length of its code**, then add. Compare against 7 bits per character for ASCII, and subtract for the saving.

tips.title: Left is 0, right is 1
tips.body: Read a Huffman code by walking from the **root** to the character's leaf, writing 0 for each left branch and 1 for each right. When decoding, go back to the root after **every** character.

tips.title: Does the tree travel with the file?
tips.body: The decoder cannot read the bits without the tree or code table, so it is stored alongside the data. That overhead is why Huffman pays off on long files and barely helps on short ones. It is usually the evaluation mark.

steps.title: Why files are compressed
steps.body:
**Compression** means storing the same information in **fewer bits**. Nothing is thrown away by the two methods on this specification: the original can be rebuilt exactly.

It matters for three reasons, and an exam answer usually wants two of them:

- **Storage.** A smaller file takes less room on a disk or a phone.
- **Transmission.** Fewer bits take less time to send, and use less of a mobile data allowance.
- **Cost.** Less bandwidth and less storage to pay for, which is why streaming services care.

AQA asks for exactly two methods: **run length encoding** and **Huffman coding**. Both spot **repetition** and store it more cleverly.

steps.title: Run length encoding
steps.body:
**Run length encoding** looks for **runs**: the same value repeated. It replaces each run with a **frequency/data pair**, which is how many times, followed by what.

A row of black and white pixels like **1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0** becomes **3 1, 2 0, 4 1, 1 0**: three 1s, two 0s, four 1s, one 0.

Check the frequencies add up to the length of the original. That single check catches most mistakes.

check.solution: Three runs: two 1s, three 0s, then one 1. That is **3** pairs: 2 1, 3 0, 1 1.

steps.title: When run length encoding fails
steps.body:
RLE only helps when there are **long runs**. Give it something that keeps changing and it makes the file **bigger**.

Take **abcabc**. Every run is one character long, so it encodes as **1a 1b 1c 1a 1b 1c**: 6 pairs to store 6 characters, and each pair needs a frequency **as well as** the character. The file has roughly doubled.

That is why RLE is used for **simple images** with blocks of one colour, such as icons, scans of black-and-white documents and fax images, and not for photographs or ordinary English text.

steps.title: Huffman coding: short codes for common characters
steps.body:
Ordinary text stores every character in the same number of bits: **7 bits** each in ASCII, whether the character is an **e** or a **z**.

Huffman coding gives the **most common** characters the **shortest** codes and the rare ones longer codes. Because the common ones appear so often, the total comes out much smaller.

The codes are read off a **Huffman tree**:

- Start at the top, the **root**.
- Every branch to the **left** is a **0**, every branch to the **right** is a **1**.
- Write the bits down as you walk to the character's **leaf**. That string of bits is its code.

No code is ever the start of another code, which is what lets a decoder read a long string of bits back without any separators between the characters.

props.caption: Left is 0, right is 1. The code is under each leaf.

visuals.alt: A Huffman tree for the word banana. The root splits to the letter a on the left with code 0, and on the right to a branch that splits to b with code 10 and n with code 11.

check.prompt: In a Huffman tree, which characters end up with the shortest codes?
check.solution: The **most common** characters sit nearest the root, so their codes are shortest. That is what makes the total number of bits small.

steps.title: Building the tree and counting the bits
steps.body:
The tree is built from the **frequencies**. Repeatedly take the **two smallest** and join them under a new branch whose weight is their total, until one tree is left.

Here is **mississippi**: i 4, s 4, p 2, m 1.

steps.title: Going deeper: choosing the method, and the hidden cost
steps.body:
Two points separate a top answer.

**The tree has to be stored too.** The decoder cannot read the bits without knowing the codes, so the tree or code table travels with the compressed data. On a short message that overhead can wipe out the saving, which is why Huffman pays off on **long** files where the same tree serves thousands of characters.

**The methods suit different data.** RLE wants **long runs of identical values**, so it is at home on simple images with blocks of one colour. Huffman wants **uneven frequencies**, which is exactly what ordinary text has: e and t everywhere, q and z almost never. On text that keeps changing, RLE makes the file bigger while Huffman still makes a substantial saving. The 72% saved on *mississippi* is unusually high because that word uses only four different letters; on ordinary English prose Huffman saves nearer 40%.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Compression** stores the same information in fewer bits, saving storage, transmission time and cost.
- **Run length encoding** replaces runs of the same value with **frequency/data pairs**, so 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0 becomes 3 1, 2 0, 4 1, 1 0.
- Check that the RLE frequencies **add up** to the length of the original.
- RLE makes data **larger** when there are no long runs, because each pair costs a frequency as well as a value.
- **Huffman coding** gives common characters short codes. Read a code off the tree by walking from the root, **left is 0 and right is 1**.
- Build the tree by repeatedly joining the **two smallest** frequencies under a new branch.
- Compressed size is **frequency × code length**, added up. Uncompressed ASCII is **7 bits per character**.
- mississippi: 21 bits compressed against 77 in ASCII, a saving of **56 bits**.
- The **tree must be stored too**, so Huffman pays off most on long files.

questions.prompt: A text file holds the word mississippi. Explain how Huffman coding compresses it, and calculate how many bits are saved compared with ASCII.
questions.solution: Huffman coding starts by counting how often each character appears: m once, p twice, i four times and s four times. The two lowest frequencies are repeatedly joined under a new branch carrying their total, until a single tree is left, so the most common characters finish nearest the root and get the shortest codes. Reading the tree with left as 0 and right as 1 gives s as 0, i as 11, m as 100 and p as 101. The compressed size is found by multiplying each frequency by the length of its code and adding the results: four times one is four, four times two is eight, two times three is six and one times three is three, which is twenty one bits in total. In ASCII every character takes seven bits, so eleven characters take seventy seven bits. The saving is seventy seven minus twenty one, which is fifty six bits, although the tree itself must be stored with the file.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Counting first.** Huffman coding counts how often each character appears: **m** once, **p** twice, **i** four times, **s** four times.

**Building the tree.** The **two lowest** frequencies are joined under a new branch carrying their total, and that repeats until one tree is left. The effect is that the **most common** characters finish **nearest the root**, so they get the **shortest** codes.

**Reading the codes.** Walking down from the root, left as 0 and right as 1, gives $s = 0$, $i = 11$, $m = 100$, $p = 101$.

**The compressed size** is frequency × code length, added up:

$$(4 \times 1) + (4 \times 2) + (2 \times 3) + (1 \times 3) = 4 + 8 + 6 + 3 = 21 \text{ bits}$$

**The uncompressed size** is 7 bits per character in ASCII:

$$11 \times 7 = 77 \text{ bits}$$

**The saving** is $77 - 21 = \mathbf{56}$ **bits**, about three quarters of the original. The tree itself must be stored with the file, which eats into that saving on a message this short.

questions.prompt: Compare run length encoding with Huffman coding. For each, describe the kind of data it suits and one situation where it would be a poor choice.
questions.solution: Run length encoding replaces runs of identical values with frequency and data pairs, so it suits data with long runs such as a simple icon or a black and white scan where large areas are one colour. It is a poor choice for a photograph or for ordinary English text, because the values change constantly, every run is one long, and storing a frequency alongside each value makes the file larger than it was. Huffman coding gives short bit codes to the characters that appear most often, so it suits ordinary text where some characters such as e and t are far more common than q and z. It is a poor choice when every character appears about equally often, since no code can then be much shorter than the rest, and on a very short message, because the tree or code table has to be stored alongside the data and can cost more than the compression saves.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Run length encoding** replaces each run of identical values with a **frequency/data pair**. It suits data with **long runs**: a simple icon, a logo, or a black and white scan where large areas are a single colour.

It is a **poor choice** for a photograph or for ordinary English text. The values change constantly, so nearly every run is one long, and storing a frequency beside each value makes the file **larger** than the original.

**Huffman coding** gives the **most common** characters the **shortest** bit codes. That suits ordinary text, where **e** and **t** appear far more often than **q** and **z**, so the short codes get used over and over.

It is a **poor choice** when every character appears about **equally often**, because no code can then be much shorter than the rest and there is little to gain. It also struggles on a **very short message**: the tree or code table must be stored alongside the data, and that overhead can cost more than the compression saves.

examTechnique.body:
Huffman questions nearly always end in a calculation, and the calculation is always the same shape: **frequency × code length**, added up, then compared with **7 bits per character** for ASCII. Write both numbers down even when only the saving is asked for, because the method marks live there.

Read codes off the tree carefully. Left is 0 and right is 1, and the code ends at a leaf. When decoding, return to the **root** after every character; students who carry on down the tree get nonsense.

For run length encoding, write the pairs as **frequency then data**, and check the frequencies add up to the length of the original. Include the runs of length one: they still need a pair.

AQA asks for these two methods only. There is no need to write about lossy or lossless compression, and doing so wastes time that the calculation marks need.
examinerErrors: Forgetting that a run of one still needs a pair, so 1c is written as just c.
Writing RLE pairs the wrong way round. The frequency comes first, then the data.
Adding the code lengths instead of multiplying each by its frequency.
Using 8 bits per character for ASCII. Standard ASCII is 7 bits; 8 is extended ASCII.
Giving the compressed size when the question asked for the saving, or the other way round.
Carrying on down the tree when decoding instead of returning to the root after each character.
Forgetting that the tree or code table must be stored alongside the compressed data.
Claiming run length encoding always makes a file smaller. On data that keeps changing it makes it larger.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer builds the tree by repeatedly joining the two lowest frequencies, explains that this puts the common characters nearest the root, and reads the codes off correctly with left as 0 and right as 1. It shows both bit calculations, frequency × code length for the compressed size and 7 bits per character for ASCII, and subtracts to give the saving. On evaluation it names the data each method suits, points out that RLE can enlarge a file with no long runs, and remembers that the Huffman tree has to be stored with the data, so short messages gain little.
